4Validate Before You Build

This chapter can save you months. Validation means finding out whether real people want your idea, and will pay for it, before you spend weeks building it. Most failed digital products did not fail because they were poorly made. They failed because nobody wanted them, or because nobody knew they existed.

What validation is not

Validation is not asking your mum if she likes it. It is not asking a friend "do you think this is a good idea?" and hearing "yes!" Kind people say yes to be polite. Real validation looks for evidence of behaviour: people searching for it, asking for it, paying for similar things or agreeing to buy.

Six ways to validate, from easiest to strongest

Method one: search and look. Search the topic on marketplaces, social platforms and search engines. Are people already selling similar products? Are there reviews? Do buyers say what they like and what is missing? A bit of competition is a good sign. It means people pay. No competition at all can mean no demand.

Method two: read real conversations. Look at questions in groups, forums and comment sections. Do people keep asking for something like your idea? Copy their exact words, because you will use them later.

Method three: talk to five to ten real people. Find people who match your ideal buyer. Ask them about their problem, not your product. Questions to ask:

  • "How do you handle [problem] today?"
  • "What is the hardest part?"
  • "Have you tried anything to fix it? What worked or did not?"
  • "Would you pay for a tool that made this easier? What would that be worth to you?"
  • "What would the perfect solution look like?"

Listen more than you talk. If three or four people describe the same frustration in similar words, you are onto something.

Method four: offer a free mini version. Make a one-page version of your idea and share it. Do people use it? Do they ask for more? Do they ask when the full version is coming? Requests for more are real signals.

Method five: a small preview or waitlist. Create a simple page or post describing the product, with a mockup, and invite people to join a waitlist. If very few people sign up, rethink the angle.

Method six: pre-sell. The strongest validation is a person paying before the product exists. Offer a first version at a small discount to the first five or ten buyers, and be transparent that it is a first edition. Only do this if you are confident you can deliver, you deliver on time and you offer clear refunds if you cannot. Be honest, and check the rules about taking payment in your country.

A simple validation script

Message to a potential buyer.

"Hi [Name], I am working on a simple monthly budget planner for students, a spreadsheet that works on a phone. You mentioned that managing money has been hard. Could I ask you three quick questions about how you handle it now? It would help me a lot. I will not try to sell you anything."

A follow-up after the conversation.

"Thank you so much for your time. What you said about [specific thing] was really helpful. When the first version is ready, would you like to try it free and tell me what you think?"

A pre-sale announcement.

"I am making a Weekly Revision Planner for students preparing for exams. It is a printable and a phone-friendly version, with a daily timetable and a progress tracker. The first ten people can get it at a reduced price while I finish the final touches, and I will take your feedback into account. Message me the word PLANNER if you would like details."

Signals that your idea is promising

  • People describe the problem in detail without being prompted.
  • Several people ask when it will be ready.
  • Similar products exist and sell, but reviews show gaps you can fill.
  • People are willing to give you their email, their time or their money.
  • You can describe the buyer and the problem in one clear sentence.

Signals to pause or adjust

  • People say "nice idea" but nothing else.
  • Nobody can explain the problem they have.
  • You cannot find anyone who has paid for anything similar.
  • Your audience is "everyone."
  • Free alternatives are plentiful and good, and you cannot explain how yours is different.

Adjusting is not failing. Narrow your audience, change the format or solve a more specific problem. "A planner" becomes "a planner for nurses who work night shifts."

Study your competition kindly

Look at five similar products. Note their price, their format, what buyers praise and what buyers complain about. Do not copy them. Ask: How can mine be clearer, simpler, better suited to a specific person or better presented? Your difference might be your audience, your simplicity, your design, your instructions or your honesty.

A one-page validation sheet

Fill this in before you build.

1. My idea in one sentence: 2. My ideal buyer: 3. Their problem: 4. How they solve it today: 5. What similar products exist and what buyers say: 6. Who I spoke to and what they said: 7. How many people signalled real interest: 8. What I will make first, in the smallest version:

If most of these are filled with real information, you are ready to build. If not, do a little more research first.

Your small task. Speak to three people who match your ideal buyer this week. Ask the questions above, and write down their exact words.

5Your Toolkit

You do not need a studio or a team. You need a few simple tools and good habits. Check current features, limits and prices on every tool before relying on it.

The free starter kit

What you needFree option to start with
Creating spreadsheetsA free browser-based spreadsheet tool
Creating documents and guidesA free browser-based document tool
Designing printables, covers and graphicsA free design tool with templates
Making PDFsExporting from your document or design tool
Mockup imagesFree mockup features in design tools
SellingA marketplace or a simple payment link, depending on your country
Storing filesFree cloud storage
Email listA free email tool
TrackingA free spreadsheet
SecurityA password manager and two-step verification

Marketplace or your own store?

This is one of the first big choices, so let us compare them honestly.

MarketplaceYour own store or page
BuyersBuilt in, but crowdedYou must bring them
FeesUsually listing and sales feesPayment processor fees, sometimes monthly tool fees
SetupEasier and fasterMore setup
ControlPlatform rules applyMore control
Customer dataOften limitedYou may collect emails with consent
Best forTesting quicklyBuilding a long-term brand

Many beginners start on a marketplace to learn quickly, then add their own page and email list as they grow. Check current fees, payout rules, supported countries and policies before choosing, because they change.

Payments

Check which payment methods are available and legal in your country, and how and when you will be paid. Understand fees, refund rules and any payout thresholds. Keep records of every sale. If you cannot use a certain platform in your country, look for alternatives rather than workarounds that break the rules.

AI tools

AI assistants can help you brainstorm, outline, draft and edit. They can also make mistakes and produce generic text. Use them as helpers, not as replacements for your knowledge, and never publish anything you have not read and checked. Be especially careful about facts, advice and copied wording. Check the rules of any marketplace about AI-assisted content. See How To Use ChatGPT And Claude To Build Real Income Streams and try the free AI Prompt Builder.

Keep your tools few

A common mistake is spending weeks comparing tools instead of making a product. Choose one tool for each job and begin. You can change later.

Organise your files

Create a folder called "Product Business" with subfolders: Ideas, Validation, Products, Mockups, Sales Pages, Customers, Money Records and Learning. Name files clearly, for example "BudgetPlanner-v1-2026-03." Keep backups in at least two places.

6Build A Simple First Version

Now we build. The goal is a minimum viable product, which means the smallest version that genuinely helps someone and can be tested. It is not your final masterpiece.

Define the promise

Write one sentence: "This product helps [who] to [achieve what] in [how long or how easily]."

Example: "This planner helps students organise their exam revision into a clear weekly timetable in ten minutes."

Everything you include should serve that promise. If it does not, leave it out.

Decide what is in and out

List everything you could include, then circle only what is essential for the promise. A smaller, clearer product is easier to use, easier to explain and easier to finish.

Plan the structure

Sketch the layout before you design it. For a spreadsheet, list the tabs and what each one does. For a printable, list the pages. For a guide, outline the chapters and the key point of each. For a template pack, list the templates and the sizes.

Make it easy to use

  • Instructions. Include a short "start here" page that explains what the product is, how to use it and what to do if something goes wrong.
  • Clear labels and examples. Fill a sample version so buyers can see how it works.
  • Consistent design. Use two or three colours and one or two fonts.
  • Readable text. Large enough, with good contrast.
  • Works on the devices people use. If you say it works on a phone, test it on a phone.
  • File naming and format. Provide formats people can open easily, such as PDF for printables, and a clear way to make a personal copy of a spreadsheet.

Respect licences and originality

Only use images, fonts, icons and templates that you have the right to use commercially, and read the licence terms. Do not copy other sellers' designs or text. Do not use brand names, characters or logos that are not yours. Do not use text from books, courses or articles without permission. When in doubt, create it yourself or check the licence. Marketplaces may remove listings and penalise accounts for copyright issues.

Test with real people

Give your first version to three to five people who match your ideal buyer. Ask them to use it without your help, and watch where they get stuck. Questions to ask:

  • "Was it clear what to do first?"
  • "What confused you?"
  • "What did you like?"
  • "What was missing?"
  • "Would you use it again?"
  • "What would you pay for it?"

Fix the biggest problems first. Small improvements add up.

The quality checklist

Before you sell, check:

Your small task. Write your one-sentence promise, list what is in and out and sketch the structure of your first version.

7How To Build Each Type, Step By Step

Different products need slightly different building steps. Here is a walk-through for the four types most beginners start with. Use the one that matches your idea, and skim the rest for ideas.

Building a spreadsheet template

What it is. A pre-built spreadsheet with structure, labels and sometimes formulas, so the buyer only has to fill in their own numbers. Budgets, trackers, planners, invoices and schedules are common examples.

Step one: write the job it must do. For example: "Show a student how much they spent and how much is left, by category, each month."

Step two: sketch the tabs on paper. One tab for inputs, one for a summary and one for instructions is a common, easy-to-understand pattern. Keep the number of tabs small.

Step three: build the inputs. Make clear boxes for the buyer to fill in. Use a consistent colour for "type here" cells, and explain the colour on the instructions tab.

Step four: add simple formulas. Sums, differences and percentages are usually enough. Test each formula with made-up numbers, including zeros and large amounts, to make sure it behaves.

Step five: protect what should not be changed. Many spreadsheet tools let you lock cells that contain formulas, so buyers do not accidentally overwrite them. Leave input cells unlocked. Check current features.

Step six: add an example. Include a filled-in sample tab, or a separate sample copy, so buyers see how it looks when used.

Step seven: write clear instructions. Explain how to make a personal copy, since many tools require the buyer to copy the file rather than edit your original. Test this on a fresh account to make sure the steps are right.

Step eight: test on a phone and a computer. Check that it opens, scrolls and calculates properly on both.

Common pitfalls. Formulas that break when a row is added, tabs that are confusing, no instructions on how to copy the file and designs that look fine on your screen but are unreadable on a phone.

Building a printable planner or checklist

What it is. A page or set of pages designed to be printed and filled in by hand.

Step one: decide the size. Many buyers print on standard letter or A4 paper, and some prefer smaller formats. Provide sizes your buyers use, and test printing.

Step two: design with margins and ink in mind. Leave generous margins so printers do not cut off edges. Use light backgrounds, because heavy colour uses a lot of ink and prints poorly at home.

Step three: make writing space generous. Lines and boxes should be large enough for real handwriting. Test by filling one in yourself.

Step four: keep a clear hierarchy. Titles, sections and instructions should be easy to tell apart. Use two fonts at most.

Step five: check contrast and readability. Print a page in black and white. If it is hard to read, adjust.

Step six: export as a PDF. PDF keeps the layout stable on different devices. Name the file clearly.

Step seven: consider a digital version. Many buyers like to fill in on a tablet or phone. If you offer this, test it properly.

Step eight: write printing tips. A short note about paper size and print settings reduces support messages.

Common pitfalls. Text too small, margins too tight, images with low resolution that look blurry and designs that waste ink.

Building a short guide or ebook

What it is. A written document that teaches something specific and is delivered as a PDF.

Step one: define the single outcome. "After reading this guide, you will be able to [specific thing]." One outcome per guide.

Step two: outline in five to eight sections. Each section should lead the reader one step closer to the outcome. Start broad, then get practical.

Step three: write plainly. Short sentences, simple words and real examples. Imagine you are teaching one friend.

Step four: include exercises or checklists. People value guides that help them do something, not only read.

Step five: add visuals where they help. Tables, simple diagrams and screenshots can make steps clear. Make sure you own or have licences for every image.

Step six: check facts and avoid risky claims. Be careful in health, money, legal and safety topics. Do not give advice you are not qualified to give, and be honest about limits.

Step seven: edit. Read aloud, cut what is not needed, and fix spelling and layout. Ask a tester to read it and tell you what is unclear.

Step eight: design a clean layout. Consistent headings, readable font size, plenty of white space and page numbers. Export as PDF.

Common pitfalls. Trying to cover everything, copying from other sources, vague advice with no steps and long blocks of text.

Building a design template pack

What it is. A set of ready-made designs, such as social media posts, highlight covers or presentation slides, that buyers can edit in a design tool.

Step one: choose a clear niche. "Social media templates for bakeries" is easier to sell than "social media templates."

Step two: set a visual style. Pick two or three colours and two fonts, and keep them consistent across the pack.

Step three: design a core set. Many buyers like a pack of ten to thirty pieces with a mix of layouts: announcements, offers, quotes and tips.

Step four: make them easy to edit. Use clearly labelled text boxes, simple layouts and editable colours. Avoid complicated effects that break when edited.

Step five: check licences thoroughly. Fonts and images often have restrictions for resale. Use only elements you are allowed to include in a product you sell, or ask buyers to add their own images. Many marketplaces have strict rules about this.

Step six: create clear delivery instructions. Explain how to open the templates, and how to make a personal copy.

Step seven: make mockups. Show examples of the templates filled in, in realistic settings.

Step eight: test with real users. Ask someone unfamiliar with design tools to edit one. Fix whatever confuses them.

Common pitfalls. Licence problems, designs that only work with the original text, no instructions and templates that look good in mockups but are hard to edit.

A few rules that apply to every type

1. One product, one promise. If you cannot say what it does in one sentence, simplify. 2. Instructions are part of the product. A short "Start Here" page prevents most support problems. 3. Test with people who are not you. You already know how it works. They do not. 4. Keep a master copy. Store your original source files safely and never send them to customers by accident. 5. Version your files. Name them clearly, such as "RevisionPlanner-v1" and "RevisionPlanner-v2." 6. Check everything twice before you publish. Spelling, numbers, links and licences.

8A Sample Sales Page, Written Out

Reading about a sales page helps. Seeing one helps more. Here is a made-up sales page in text form for a Weekly Revision Planner. Adapt the structure to your own product, and use your own words.

Headline. A Weekly Revision Planner For Students Who Do Not Know Where To Start

Opening. Exams are coming, your notes are everywhere and every time you sit down you wonder what to revise first. You are not lazy. You just need a plan that fits on one page.

What it is. The Weekly Revision Planner helps you turn your subjects and exam dates into a simple weekly timetable in about ten minutes. Print it, or fill it in on your phone.

What you get.

  • A printable weekly planner, in two common paper sizes.
  • A phone-friendly digital version you can type into.
  • A subject tracker to see what you have covered.
  • An exam countdown page.
  • A "Start Here" page with a five-step guide and a worked example.

How it works.

1. Download the file. 2. List your subjects and exam dates. 3. Fill in your weekly timetable. 4. Tick off topics as you revise.

Who it is for. Students preparing for school or college exams who want a clear, simple plan.

Who it is not for. If you want a long course on study techniques, this is not that. It is a planner, not a programme.

What testers said. "I stopped feeling lost on Sundays." "It took me ten minutes to set up and I actually used it." (Use only real feedback, with permission.)

Questions. Does it work on a phone? Yes, the digital version is designed for phone screens. Can I print it more than once? Yes, for your own personal use. Can I share it with friends? Please ask them to download their own copy, so I can keep making products like this.

Price and promise. [Price]. If the file does not open or does not work as described, message me and I will fix it or refund you, according to the platform's rules.

Call to action. Download your planner today and start your timetable tonight.

What to notice

The page names the problem in the buyer's words, describes exactly what is included, shows a simple process, is honest about who it is not for and makes a clear, fair promise. It does not exaggerate. It does not invent results.

9Price It

Pricing makes beginners nervous, so let us make it calm and practical. The aim is a price that is fair to the buyer and profitable for you.

The three things that shape a price

Value to the buyer. What is the problem worth solving? A budget planner that helps someone avoid overdraft fees may be worth more to them than its cost. A prettier wall poster may be worth less.

The market. What do similar products sell for? Look at five of them. Price is a signal, and being much cheaper can signal low quality, while being much higher needs strong reasons.

Your costs and goals. What must each sale cover: tools, fees, your time and your profit?

Count your fees

Every sale has costs. Marketplaces may charge a listing fee and a percentage of the sale. Payment processors charge a percentage and sometimes a fixed fee per sale. Tools may have monthly fees. Check the current figures for the platforms you use.

Here is a made-up calculation to show the idea.

ItemAmount
Price the customer pays12.00
Platform fee (example 10%)1.20
Payment fee (example 3% plus 0.30)0.66
What you receive before other costs10.14

If your tools cost a monthly amount, divide it by the number of sales to see the cost per sale. If you made fewer sales than you hoped, your profit per sale is smaller than it looks. Knowing this stops you from celebrating revenue while losing money.

How many sales do you need?

Work backwards. Suppose you want your product to cover your monthly tool costs and give a small profit. Divide your goal by the amount you receive per sale. If you receive about ten per sale and want to earn a hundred a month, you need ten sales. Then ask: how many people must see the product for ten to buy? If two percent of visitors buy, you need about five hundred visitors. Seeing the numbers shows you whether your plan is realistic.

Choose a starting price

For a first product, a modest, clear price is usually easier to sell than a high one, because buyers do not yet know you. Many beginners start with a low or moderate price and raise it as they collect reviews and improve the product. Do not start so low that you cannot cover your costs, and do not price based on fear.

Pricing structures

One price. Simple and clear.

Tiers. For example, a basic version and a deluxe version with extras. The middle or highest tier often helps people see value.

Bundles. Several related products for a better combined price. A bundle can raise your average sale.

Launch pricing. A time-limited introductory price, honestly presented. Do not use fake countdowns or invented "original prices." Be truthful, because dishonest pricing breaks trust and can break the law in some countries.

Pay what you want or free versions. Sometimes used for lead magnets, which are free gifts that attract email subscribers.

Test and adjust

You can change your price. Watch your results: if many people view but few buy, the problem may be the page, the trust or the price. If everyone buys immediately and says it is a bargain, the price may be too low. Make one change at a time, give it a fair test and record the results.

Refunds and guarantees

Decide your refund policy before you launch, and check the rules of your marketplace and your country, because some places require certain consumer rights. A clear, fair policy builds trust. Digital goods often have special rules, so read them carefully.

Your small task. Write your fees per sale, your starting price and how many sales you would need to reach your first small goal.

10Sales Page And Delivery

A sales page is the page that explains your product and invites people to buy. It can be a marketplace listing or a page on your own site. Its job is to answer a stranger's questions quickly and honestly.

What a stranger wants to know

1. What is this? 2. Is it for me? 3. What will I get? 4. How will it help me? 5. Can I trust you? 6. How much is it, and what if I do not like it? 7. How do I buy it?

Your page should answer these in order, in plain words.

The anatomy of a good sales page

A clear headline. Say what it is and who it is for. "A weekly revision planner for exam students."

A short opening. Name the problem in the buyer's words. "Exams are coming and your notes are everywhere."

What is included. A bullet list of exactly what the buyer receives, including file types and number of pages.

Pictures. Clear mockups showing the product in use. Show several angles. Make sure images do not mislead, and show real content, not just a pretty cover.

How it works. Three simple steps: download, personalise, use.

Who it is for, and who it is not for. Honesty builds trust.

Proof. Testimonials from testers or buyers, with permission, or honest notes from the testing stage. Do not invent reviews.

Frequently asked questions. Answer the common ones: Does it work on a phone? Can I print it? Can I edit it? What if I need help?

Price and refund policy. Clear and visible.

A call to action. A button or instruction, such as "Download now."

A sales page copy formula

Use this structure and fill in your own words.

1. The problem: "Studying for exams feels overwhelming when you do not know what to revise or when." 2. The promise: "This weekly planner helps you build a clear revision timetable in ten minutes." 3. What you get: "A printable and a phone-friendly version, a subject tracker and an exam countdown page." 4. Why it works: "It breaks big goals into small daily tasks." 5. Who it is for: "Students preparing for exams who want a simple plan." 6. What others say: "Testers said it helped them stop feeling lost." 7. How to get it: "Instant download. Print it or use it on your phone." 8. Our promise: "If it does not work as described, contact me within [days] and I will help or refund, according to the platform's rules."

Write in your buyer's language

Use the exact words people used when you spoke to them. Avoid jargon. Be specific rather than vague. "Fits on one page" is better than "comprehensive."

Product photos and mockups

Show the product in a realistic setting: a printed page on a desk, a spreadsheet on a phone, a guide on a tablet. Keep the style consistent. Include a close-up of the actual contents. Make the first image especially clear, because it appears in search results.

Delivery

Delivery means how the buyer receives the product after paying. Typically it is an instant download link, an email with a link or access to an online page. Check that:

  • The file opens easily on common devices.
  • The file size is reasonable.
  • The instructions are clear.
  • Buyers can re-download if they lose the file.
  • You have a way to help if something fails.

Test the whole buying experience yourself. Buy your own product, or have a friend do it, and note every step.

Customer emails

A short, friendly delivery email builds trust. For example:

"Hi [Name], thank you for your order! Your Weekly Revision Planner is attached below. Start with the 'Start Here' page, which takes two minutes. If anything is unclear, reply to this email and I will help. I hope it makes your revision feel lighter. Warm regards, Ruth."

If your platform sends automatic messages, check what the buyer sees and add your own friendly note if possible.

Terms and policies

On your own page, include clear terms: what the buyer may do with the product (the licence), what they may not do (resell or share it), your refund policy and how you handle their data. Many countries have privacy and consumer laws. I am not a lawyer, so please check the rules that apply to you and your buyers, and consider getting advice for your own store.

Licence wording, in plain language

Be clear on what buyers may do. Common wording:

  • Personal use: "You may print and use this for yourself and your family."
  • No resale: "You may not share, resell or redistribute the file."
  • Commercial use: If you allow it, say exactly how, such as using a template for client work, but not reselling the template itself.

Your small task. Draft your sales page using the formula above. Read it aloud and ask a friend to tell you what the product is in one sentence.

11Legal, Tax And Money Basics

This is the less glamorous part, and it protects you. I am not a lawyer, tax adviser or accountant, so please treat this as a checklist of things to look into, not as advice.

Check your local rules

Look at official government and small business websites for your country. Questions to explore:

  • Do I need to register as a business or sole trader to sell online?
  • Do I need a licence for any type of product?
  • How is online income taxed, and when do I have to report it?
  • Are there rules about collecting sales tax or value-added tax on digital goods, in my country or the buyer's?
  • Are there consumer protection rules about refunds, pricing and advertising claims?
  • Are there privacy and data protection rules when I collect emails or customer information?

Rules vary widely and change, so check them from official sources and consider speaking to a qualified person, especially as you grow.

Intellectual property

You own what you create, but you must also respect what others own. Keep records of your licences for fonts, images and tools. Do not copy. Avoid brand names and characters. If someone copies your work, check the marketplace's reporting tools.

Records and money

Keep invoices, receipts, sales reports and payment statements. Record income and expenses in a simple spreadsheet each week. Set aside part of each payment for taxes until you know your obligations. Consider keeping business money in a separate account or pot.

Customer data and privacy

If you collect emails or any personal information, get clear consent, tell people what you will do with it, keep it secure and let them unsubscribe easily. Do not share or sell personal data.

Honest claims

Do not make promises you cannot keep. Avoid exaggerated claims about results, especially in areas such as health, money and legal matters. Be careful with before and after claims, testimonials and "guaranteed" language. Check advertising rules.

Insurance and bigger steps

As your business grows, you may want advice about business structure, insurance, contracts and accounting. Start simple, and add professional help as income justifies it.

For a full lesson on money habits, read Budget Like A Queen and use the free Personal Budget Planner.

12Launch To Real Buyers

A launch is simply the period when you tell people your product exists and invite them to buy. It does not need fireworks. It needs a clear plan, honest communication and a small group of real people to tell.

Before launch: the readiness checklist

Who to tell first: your warm network and early audience

The first buyers usually come from people who already know you or already follow you. Make a list of fifty people who might benefit, or who know someone who might. Include friends, family, colleagues, community members and anyone who has shown interest in your validation stage, such as those on your waitlist.

Never pressure anyone. Share, explain who it is for and make it easy to say no. Ask for feedback and referrals as much as for sales.

A fourteen-day launch plan

Here is a gentle plan you can adapt. It assumes about thirty to sixty minutes a day.

Days 1 to 3: warm up. Share content about the problem your product solves. Tell a short story, share a tip or post a question. Do not sell yet. Let people see that you are working on something.

Day 4: announce. Tell your audience and warm network that your product is coming and when. Invite them to join a waitlist or message you.

Days 5 to 6: show. Share a sneak peek: a screenshot, a short video of how it works or a testimonial from a tester, with permission.

Day 7: open the doors. Launch. Share your sales page link, a clear description and a special introductory offer if you have one, honestly stated.

Days 8 to 10: answer and remind. Reply to questions, share more examples and show how others are using it. Follow up with your waitlist.

Days 11 to 12: share proof. Share feedback and results, with permission, and address common questions.

Day 13: last call, if there is a real deadline. Only say "last chance" if it is true.

Day 14: review. Count your numbers: visitors, messages, sales and feedback. Write what worked, what did not and what you will change.

Scripts for your launch

A message to your warm network.

"Hi [Name], I have been working on something and I would love your honest thoughts. I made a simple Weekly Revision Planner for students preparing for exams, in a printable and a phone-friendly version. If you know anyone who is revising, I would be so grateful if you shared it. Here is the link: [link]. No pressure at all."

A post announcing the product.

"Exams are coming, and I know how overwhelming revision can feel. So I made something to help. The Weekly Revision Planner gives you a clear timetable in ten minutes, with a subject tracker and exam countdown. It is available now through the link in my bio. If you have questions, message me the word PLANNER and I will help."

A story or short video idea. Show the problem (messy notes), then the solution (the planner in use), and end with a clear invitation.

A reply to someone asking about it.

"Thank you for asking! The planner is a printable and a phone-friendly version, so you can use it either way. It takes about ten minutes to set up. Here is the link: [link]. If you have any problems opening it, message me and I will help."

A message to a community admin, asking permission to share.

"Hello, I made a simple revision planner for students and I think your members might find it useful. Would it be okay to share it in the group, or would you prefer I did not? I understand if there are rules against promotion."

Always follow group rules, and never spam.

A follow-up to your waitlist.

"Hi [Name], you joined my waitlist for the revision planner, and it is ready! Here is the link: [link]. As a thank you for waiting, here is an introductory price until [date]. Thank you for your support."

A thank-you and request for feedback after purchase.

"Thank you so much for buying the planner! If you have a moment after using it, I would love to hear what worked and what could be better. Your feedback helps me improve it for everyone."

After the first sale

Celebrate, then learn. Ask the buyer why they bought. Ask what almost stopped them. Ask what they hoped to get. Their answers are marketing gold, because they tell you what matters to real buyers.

13Where To Go: Finding Buyers

You now have a product. The question is where the right people will find it. You do not need all of these places. Choose your warm network, plus two or three, and stay consistent for at least a month.

Your warm network (start here)

Your warm network is everyone who knows you: family, friends, classmates, colleagues, neighbours and community groups. They are your first buyers, your first testers and your first sharers. Many digital products get their first sales this way. Ask for honest feedback and introductions, not favours.

Marketplaces

A marketplace is a website where buyers browse many sellers' digital products. It brings built-in traffic and handles payment, for a fee. Good titles, clear photos and relevant keywords matter. Check current fees and policies, and remember that listing a product does not guarantee it will be found.

Instagram

Instagram suits visual products such as planners, templates and printables. Share short videos of the product in use, behind-the-scenes posts, tips related to the problem it solves and customer feedback. Invite people to message a keyword for the link. Read Instagram Pays Too, Sis for a full guide.

TikTok

Short, useful videos can reach people who do not know you. Show a quick tip, a before and after or how you use your product. Check each platform's rules about promotion, and be wary of anyone promising overnight sales.

Pinterest

Pinterest works like a visual search engine. People look for ideas, planners, templates and printables. Pins that link to your product page or blog can bring steady traffic over time. It rewards clear titles, good images and patience.

YouTube

Short tutorials or demonstrations about the problem your product solves can attract viewers who are actively searching. It is slower to start but can bring long-term traffic. See The Soft Girl's Guide To Becoming A Full-Time YouTube Creator.

LinkedIn

LinkedIn suits products for professionals, freelancers and small businesses, such as templates, checklists and guides. Share helpful posts and connect with people who might benefit. See Babe, Your Next International Opportunity Is On LinkedIn.

X (formerly Twitter)

Useful for sharing short tips and joining conversations. Some creators sell templates and guides to their followers. Keep it helpful rather than pushy.

Facebook groups

Groups exist for almost every niche. Read the rules, help others and share your product only where promotion is allowed. Avoid groups full of "get rich quick" posts.

Reddit

Communities exist for many topics. Many ban self-promotion. Contribute honestly, answer questions and share your product only when rules allow and it genuinely helps.

Your own email list

An email list is the most valuable place you can build. People on it chose to hear from you. Offer a free gift, such as a one-page checklist, in exchange for an email address, and send helpful emails regularly. Check your country's rules about consent and unsubscribing.

Search engines and blogs

If you write helpful articles about the problem your product solves, people who search for answers can find you. It is slow, but it can bring steady visitors for years.

Partnerships

Collaborate with people who serve the same audience in a different way. A tutor might share a revision planner. A wedding planner might share a budget sheet. Offer to help them, and agree on honest terms, including disclosure if there are affiliate links or payments.

Local and in-person

If your product suits a local audience, such as schools, small businesses or community groups, a friendly introduction can work wonders.

How to choose

Ask: Where do my buyers already spend time? Where can I show up weekly without dreading it? Choose your warm network, a marketplace and one or two others.

14Marketing That Does Not Feel Pushy

Marketing is simply helping the right people discover something that could help them. Here is a gentle way to do it.

Teach first, sell second

Share useful tips related to the problem your product solves. For example, if you sell a budget planner, share a short tip about how to track spending. People who find your tips helpful will naturally be curious about your product.

Show the product in use

Short videos, screenshots and real examples show what the product does far better than a long description.

Answer real questions

Reply to comments, messages and community questions. Each answer helps someone and shows your expertise.

Use testimonials honestly

Ask happy buyers for a short quote and permission to share it. Never invent or edit testimonials. Do not offer payment for positive reviews if the rules forbid it.

Use a content rhythm you can keep

A simple pattern: two tips, one product post and one story each week. Batch your content in one session so it does not take over your life.

Use keywords

On marketplaces and search engines, use the words your buyers use. If they search for "weekly revision planner printable," use those words in your title and description, naturally and honestly.

Track what works

Note which posts, platforms and keywords lead to visits and sales. Do more of what works. Stop what does not.

Disclose properly

If you use affiliate links or paid partnerships, say so clearly, according to the rules in your country and on each platform.

15Build And Use An Email List

An email list is the one asset in this business that you truly own. Platforms change their rules, algorithms shift and accounts can be limited, but people who chose to hear from you stay reachable. Let us build one properly.

What an email list is and why it matters

An email list is a group of people who have given you permission to send them emails. A lead magnet is a free, useful item that you offer in exchange for an email address, such as a one-page checklist. A welcome sequence is a short series of emails that new subscribers receive automatically. A newsletter is a regular email sent to everyone on your list.

Email matters because it reaches people directly. When you launch a new product, you can tell people who already trust you. Compared with social media posts that may be seen by a small fraction of followers, an email arrives in an inbox people check.

Permission and rules

Only add people who have clearly agreed. Do not copy emails from groups or buy lists. Tell people what they are signing up for and how often you will write. Include a simple way to unsubscribe in every email. Rules about email marketing, consent and data protection differ by country, so please check what applies where you and your subscribers live. I am not a lawyer, and this is an area where the rules matter.

Create your lead magnet

A good lead magnet is small, specific and quick to use. Ideas:

  • A one-page checklist related to your product's problem.
  • A short sample of your planner or template.
  • A mini-guide of five tips.
  • A simple tracker that solves one tiny problem.

The best lead magnets give a quick win and hint at the larger product. For example, a free one-week revision timetable could lead to your full revision planner.

Set up a simple sign-up

Use a free email tool and create a simple sign-up page or form. Write a clear promise: "Get a free one-week revision timetable, plus one study tip a week." Place the link in your bio, your sales page and your posts. Test it yourself.

A simple welcome sequence

Here is a made-up three-email sequence for a revision planner business. Adjust the content to your own product.

Email one: sent immediately.

Subject: Your free revision timetable is here

"Hi [Name], thank you for joining! Here is your free one-week revision timetable: [link]. To use it, list your subjects, fill in your exam dates and choose two topics a day. If you get stuck, reply to this email and tell me where, and I will help. Warm regards, Ruth."

Email two: sent two days later.

Subject: One mistake that makes revision harder

"Hi [Name], the most common revision mistake I see is trying to study everything at once. Here is a simple way to choose what to revise first: [short, useful tip]. If you want a full plan you can print or use on your phone, my Weekly Revision Planner is here: [link]. No pressure. Just sharing in case it helps."

Email three: sent five days later.

Subject: How other students use the planner

"Hi [Name], a student told me she sets up her planner on Sunday evenings and finishes in ten minutes. Here is how she does it: [short story, with permission]. If you would like to try it, here is the link: [link]. And if you have a question, just reply. I read every email."

Keep emails short, kind and useful. One idea per email.

The newsletter rhythm

Once a week or every two weeks is plenty. A simple format: one useful tip, one short story or update, and one gentle mention of your product or a new offer. If you have nothing new to sell, share something helpful. Trust is built in the emails where you do not ask for anything.

Measure and improve

Most email tools show how many people opened and clicked your emails. These numbers can be affected by privacy features, so treat them as rough guides. More useful questions: Did people reply? Did they click through to the product? Did sales follow? If few people open, improve your subject lines. If people open but do not click, improve your call to action.

Never spam, never mislead

Do not send misleading subject lines, fake urgency or messages that pretend to be personal when they are not. Respect people's inboxes. A smaller, engaged list beats a large, ignored one.

16Pricing Experiments You Can Run Safely

Once you have some visitors, you can learn a great deal by gently testing your price and offer. The key word is gently: change one thing at a time, give it a fair test and keep records.

What you can test

  • The price. Raise or lower it slightly.
  • The headline. Try a clearer or more specific version.
  • The main image. Try a different mockup.
  • The bundle. Offer two products together.
  • The guarantee wording. Make your refund promise clearer.
  • The introductory offer. Test a time-limited, honest discount.

How to run a fair test

1. Choose one change. If you change three things at once, you will not know which mattered. 2. Decide how you will measure it. For example, the percentage of visitors who buy. 3. Run it for long enough. A few days with ten visitors tells you almost nothing. Wait until you have a reasonable number of visitors, or run it for a few weeks. 4. Record the before and after. Write both numbers down. 5. Decide. Keep the change, undo it or try another.

A made-up example

Suppose your page gets a certain number of visitors in a month and a small number buy. You change the headline from "Weekly Planner" to "A Weekly Revision Planner For Students Who Do Not Know Where To Start." Over the next month, you notice that more visitors buy and more people mention the word "start" in messages. The change appears to help. You keep it, and make a note of it. Please remember that small numbers fluctuate a lot, so avoid dramatic conclusions from tiny samples.

Be honest about discounts

Only describe a price as a discount if it genuinely was that price before, for a real period. Do not invent a fake "original price." Do not use countdown timers that reset. Many countries have rules about misleading price claims, and buyers notice dishonesty.

Protect existing buyers

If you raise the price, people who already bought should not feel cheated. It is usually fine, because your price today does not change what they paid. If you lower it dramatically soon after launch, be thoughtful about how it affects your first buyers, and consider offering them a bonus or an upgrade.

When a price change is not the answer

If few people visit, the problem is visibility, not price. If many visit but few buy, check the page and the trust signals first. If many buy and ask for refunds, the problem is the product or the description. A price change can only fix a price problem.

17What A Healthy Week Looks Like

When you are running a small digital product business alongside a job or study, a simple weekly rhythm keeps everything moving without taking over your life. This example assumes about eight to ten hours a week. Adjust it to your own time.

DayFocusTime
MondayPlan the week: check numbers, choose three priorities30 minutes
TuesdayCreate or improve a product90 minutes
WednesdayMarketing: write and schedule content, send a newsletter90 minutes
ThursdayCustomer support and feedback, update records45 minutes
FridayOutreach: message partners, share with communities45 minutes
SaturdayLearn something new or work on the next product90 minutes
SundayRest, or a ten-minute review10 minutes

Protect your energy

Notice that Sunday is mostly rest. A business that costs you your health is not worth building. If you only have three hours a week, choose the two or three most important tasks, usually creating or improving, a small amount of marketing and customer support. Skip the rest for now.

Seasons of the year

Many digital products have natural busy times. Planners sell around the start of a year or a school term, exam materials sell before exams, wedding templates sell in wedding seasons and tax or budget tools sell around financial deadlines. Notice when your buyers need your product, and plan your content and launches a few weeks ahead. Keep a simple calendar of those moments.

A monthly review

On the last day of each month, spend thirty minutes on these questions: What did I earn and spend? Which product and platform brought buyers? What did buyers ask for? What took more time than it was worth? What will I stop, start and continue? Write the answers in one page and keep it. Over a year, these pages become your own manual for what works.

18Support Your Customers And Improve Your Product

A sale is not the end of the story. How you treat buyers after they pay shapes your reviews, your referrals and your repeat sales.

Answer promptly and kindly

Aim to reply within a day or two, even if only to say, "Thank you, I am looking into it." Keep a short list of common questions and answers, so you can reply quickly. Be patient with confused buyers. Confusion often points to something unclear in your product or page.

Handle problems well

When something goes wrong:

1. Acknowledge it. "I am sorry the file would not open." 2. Fix it fast. Send a new link, a different format or a clear instruction. 3. Offer a refund if the product did not work as described, according to your policy and platform rules. 4. Learn from it. If two people had the same problem, fix the product or the instructions.

A buyer who has a problem solved quickly often becomes your biggest fan.

Collect feedback and reviews

Ask buyers what they liked and what was missing. Invite reviews where the platform allows it, and thank everyone. Respond to negative reviews calmly and professionally, without arguing. Use criticism as free product development.

Keep a simple improvement log

Create a note called "Version history." Each time you improve the product, write the date and what changed. Update the file for existing buyers where possible, and tell them. Updates make a product feel alive and give you a reason to email your customers.

Know your numbers

Each month, record:

  • Visitors to your page, if available.
  • Sales.
  • Conversion rate (sales divided by visitors).
  • Revenue and expenses.
  • Refunds and reasons.
  • Where buyers came from.
  • Questions people asked.

Look for patterns. If many people visit but few buy, improve the page, the price or the trust signals. If few people visit, improve visibility. If many buy but ask for refunds, improve the product or the description.

19Grow From One Product To A Small Business

Once your first product is selling, you may want to grow. Let us do it sustainably.

The product ladder

A product ladder is a set of products at different price points, so buyers can start small and move up.

StepExamplePurpose
FreeA one-page checklistBuilds your email list and trust
Low priceA single template or plannerFirst purchase
Mid priceA bundle or a deluxe versionHigher value for engaged buyers
Higher priceA mini-course, workshop or personalised versionFor people who want more help

You do not need all steps. A free item and one or two products can be plenty to start.

Ways to add value

Bundles. Combine related products for a combined price. For example, a budget planner, a savings tracker and a bill calendar.

Variations. Create versions for different audiences, such as a student version and a freelancer version, if it truly helps them.

Upgrades and updates. Improve the product based on feedback and offer a new version.

Companion products. A guide that teaches people how to use your template, or a quick video walkthrough.

Services. Offer a paid setup session or a custom version. This can increase income while you learn what people want. See How To Get Your First Freelance Client.

Seasonal products. Items tied to predictable moments, such as exams, new year planning or back to school.

Choose your next product from real data

Instead of guessing, ask your buyers: "What is the next thing you wish you had?" Look at the questions they ask, the reviews and the products that sell best. Build the next product from what people ask for.

Build systems

As you add products, simple systems save time:

  • A product template. The same layout and instructions style, so each new product is quicker to make.
  • A launch checklist. The steps you follow each time.
  • A customer reply document. Saved answers to common questions.
  • A weekly rhythm. Time for creating, marketing, support and review.
  • A money routine. A fixed time each week to record sales and expenses.

Automation, carefully

Many tools can automate delivery emails, reminders and posting. Automation is useful, but test it often and never let it replace real care for customers. Check privacy and consent rules before automating anything that uses customer data.

When to consider help

When you have more work than time, you might hire a freelancer for design, customer support or admin. Do this once your processes are clear and your income can support it. Check the rules in your country about hiring and paying people, and agree on terms in writing.

Do not lose your audience

Keep showing up for your audience. Share tips, answer questions and ask what they need. A business built on real relationships survives algorithm changes and trends.

20A Complete Plan To Turn Your Product Into Income

Here is the honest sequence, from idea to steady income, with the stages when money usually arrives.

Stage one: validate and build (weeks one to six)

You do not earn yet. You learn what people want, build a first version and test it. This is also when you build your warm network list and your waitlist.

Stage two: launch (weeks six to eight)

You launch to your warm network and early audience. You earn your first sales, collect feedback and fix problems. Income is small, and the learning is large.

Stage three: promote and improve (months three to six)

You build regular visibility on one or two platforms, grow your email list and improve the product using feedback. You add a second product or a bundle based on real requests. Sales become steadier, though often still small.

Stage four: build a catalogue (months six to twelve)

You add a few products, create a simple product ladder and build systems. You may add a paid service or a higher-priced product. Income becomes more predictable.

Stage five: refine and diversify (year two onward)

You raise prices where justified, test new platforms, consider partnerships and explore other income streams such as services or affiliate links, always with honest disclosure. For ideas, see the $1,000 To $5,000 Online Income Ladder.

A made-up income stack

Take Efua, a made-up example. In year one she creates a budget planner, a savings tracker and a bundle. She offers a free one-page checklist to build her email list, sells her products on a marketplace and her own page, and offers a small paid setup session for people who want help. Her income comes from several small streams: bundle sales, individual sales and a few setup sessions. No single stream is huge, but together they make a steady side income, and she understands each one.

Set goals you control

You cannot control sales, but you can control the number of conversations you have, posts you share, emails you send, products you improve and days you show up. Set goals around those and let results follow.

21Common Mistakes (And How To Dodge Them)

Everyone makes some of these. Seeing them in advance saves you months.

Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake one is building before validating. Talk to real buyers first.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake two is making a product for "everyone." Narrow it to one clear buyer and one clear problem.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake three is waiting for perfect. Launch a good first version, then improve.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake four is ignoring licences. Check every font, image and icon, and respect others' work.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake five is underpricing without counting fees. Know what you actually keep from each sale.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake six is thinking listing equals selling. Bring your own buyers.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake seven is neglecting instructions. A confused buyer asks for a refund.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake eight is making ten products before selling one. Learn from one before building more.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake nine is ignoring customers. Their questions and reviews are your best research.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake ten is skipping records. Track income, expenses, refunds and taxes from day one.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake eleven is promoting dishonestly. Fake scarcity, invented reviews and exaggerated claims destroy trust.
Common Mistake 🚨 Mistake twelve is giving up in the quiet stage. Most small shops are quiet for a while before the first sales.

22When Things Do Not Go To Plan: A Troubleshooting Table

What is happeningWhat it usually meansWhat to try
Nobody visits my pageLow visibilityShare with your warm network, post helpful content daily on one platform and improve keywords
People visit but do not buyUnclear page, low trust or price mismatchImprove the headline, photos and description, add honest proof and test your price
I get no sales for weeksEarly stage, wrong audience or weak promotionRe-check validation, talk to ten potential buyers and promote consistently
Buyers ask for refundsProduct does not match description or is confusingImprove instructions, update the description and fix product problems
Someone copied my productIntellectual property issueKeep evidence, use the platform's reporting tools and check local rules
My product keeps getting small complaintsReal gapsFix the top issue and tell buyers about the update
I am overwhelmed by toolsToo many toolsUse a small free toolkit and ignore the rest
I cannot decide what to make nextNot enough dataAsk buyers what they want and look at your best sellers
I feel discouragedNormal in the quiet stageReview your numbers, celebrate small wins and talk to a supportive friend
I am exhaustedDoing too muchReduce your product list, batch tasks and take rest days
I made a mistake in a fileQuality control gapFix it, send an update, apologise briefly and add a check to your process
A platform changed its rulesPlatform riskRead the new terms, adapt and keep your email list so you are not dependent on one platform

23Scam And Safety Warnings

As soon as you start selling online, people will try to take advantage. Learn the patterns early.

Common scams aimed at digital sellers

  • Fake "buyer" overpayment scams. A buyer sends too much and asks you to refund the difference. The original payment later proves fake or is reversed.
  • Fake marketplace messages. Emails that look like they are from your marketplace or payment provider, asking you to log in through a link or share a code.
  • Fake collaboration offers. "Brands" or "agencies" that ask you to pay for exposure or "listing fees."
  • Fake "bulk buyers." Someone offers to buy a large amount if you move the conversation and payment off the platform.
  • Fake course and "guaranteed income" offers. Promises that you can build a six-figure digital product empire, if you pay now.
  • Fake copyright or takedown claims. Messages threatening to remove your product unless you click a link or pay.
  • Product thieves. People who copy your product and sell it as their own.
  • Phishing. Fake login pages to steal your account.
  • Fake payment proofs. Screenshots of payments that never arrived.

Warning signs

Urgency and pressure. Requests to move off the platform. Requests for your password or verification code. Offers that seem far too generous. Messages with poor spelling from addresses that do not match the real company. Anyone asking you to pay to be paid.

Safety habits

Use strong, unique passwords and two-step verification, especially for your email and your selling accounts. Never share verification codes. Keep communication and payments on the platform when the rules require it. Check payments in your own account, not through screenshots. Verify messages by logging in through the official site yourself, not through a link. Keep backups of your files and your product source documents.

If you think you have been scammed

Please do not blame yourself. Stop contact. Change your passwords immediately, starting with your email, and turn on two-step verification. Contact the platform and your payment provider quickly. Save screenshots and details. Report it to the appropriate authority in your country. Tell someone you trust.

24Worked Examples

Let us walk through three made-up examples to show how the pieces fit together. They are teaching examples, not real results.

Example one: Adaeze, a budget planner for students

The idea. Adaeze keeps a clear monthly budget and friends keep asking for her spreadsheet. She writes: "This planner helps students track their money each month in ten minutes."

Validation. She speaks to six students. Four say budgeting feels confusing, and three say they tried free templates but found them cluttered. She looks at similar products and notices that reviews often complain about complicated layouts.

Building. She makes a simple one-sheet monthly planner with a spending tracker and a savings goal, plus a "Start Here" page. Three testers use it for two weeks, and she simplifies a confusing column.

Pricing. She calculates her fees per sale and sets a modest price, with a small introductory discount for her waitlist.

Launch. She follows a fourteen-day plan. She tells her warm network, shares short videos of how it works and posts in two student groups where promotion is allowed.

Result. In the first month she makes a few sales, mostly through friends of friends. She collects feedback, improves the planner and adds a savings tracker as a second product. By month six she has an email list and three products.

Lessons. Validation, a narrow audience, testing and a patient launch.

Example two: Bisi, a content calendar for small businesses

The idea. Bisi manages social media for small shops. She notices her clients all struggle with planning content. She creates a content calendar template.

Validation. She shows it to five clients, who all say they would use it. Two offer to pay for a customised version.

Building. She makes a spreadsheet and a printable version with a monthly view and a post idea bank. She writes a short instructions page and checks fonts and icons for commercial licences.

Selling. She lists it on a marketplace and her own page. She also offers a paid setup session for those who want help.

Growth. She builds a free "thirty content ideas" checklist to grow her email list. Over several months she adds a version for salons and a version for restaurants, based on requests.

Lessons. Starting from real client questions, offering a free gift, and using a service to learn what people want.

Example three: Ngozi, who nearly made the wrong product

The idea. Ngozi loves journaling and decides to make a beautiful, complicated planner with dozens of pages. She spends two months designing it.

What goes wrong. When she shows it to potential buyers, they say it looks lovely but is overwhelming, and they would only use a few pages. She had not validated first.

What she changes. She simplifies, creates a one-week planner with a gratitude page and a habit tracker and tests it with five people. She keeps the original as a later "deluxe" version.

Result. Her smaller product sells more easily. The deluxe version becomes her second product for buyers who want more.

Lessons. A smaller, clearer product often sells better. Validate before you build.

Create your own example

Write your own story in five lines: The buyer I want to help. Their problem. The smallest version I will build first. How I will test it. The date I will launch to my warm network.

25Mindset: The Voices That Show Up

When you build something of your own, familiar voices appear. Here is how I answer them.

"Nobody will buy it." Maybe not at first. That is why you validate and test. Fewer sales than you hoped are information, not a verdict on you.

"Someone else already made this." Good. It means people pay for it. Your job is to serve a specific person better, more simply or more kindly.

"It is not good enough yet." Launch the first version, with honesty about what it is, and improve. Waiting for perfect usually means never launching.

"I am not a designer." You do not need to be. Clear, simple and useful beats fancy. You can also learn the basics, or work with a freelancer later.

"Everyone will see me fail." Most people are busy with their own lives. And the few who notice will usually respect that you tried.

"What if it takes too long?" It usually takes longer than you hope. Plan for months, build alongside your current income and celebrate small wins.

"I feel like a fraud." If you can help one person with what you know, you have something to offer. Share what you know honestly.

A digital product business starts with one useful thing and one real person it helps.

26Your First Seven Days: A Gentle Quick Start

About thirty to sixty minutes a day.

Day 1. List ten things people ask you for help with, and ten problems you have solved.

Day 2. Turn your best three ideas into product ideas using the three-circle method. Fill in the scoring table.

Day 3. Choose one idea. Write your one-sentence promise and describe your ideal buyer.

Day 4. Search for similar products. Note price, reviews and gaps.

Day 5. Talk to two people who match your ideal buyer. Write their exact words.

Day 6. Set up your folders and tools. Draft your product outline.

Day 7. Write down what you learned, adjust your idea and plan your first version.

27Your Thirty-Day Plan

Here is a full month. About thirty to sixty minutes a day. If you miss a day, simply continue.

Week one: find and shape your idea

  • Days 1 to 7: follow the quick start above.

Week two: validate and plan

  • Day 8: Speak to a third and fourth potential buyer.
  • Day 9: Study five competitor products in more detail.
  • Day 10: Fill in the one-page validation sheet.
  • Day 11: Decide what is in and out of your first version.
  • Day 12: Sketch the structure.
  • Day 13: Set up your toolkit and choose where you will sell.
  • Day 14: Review and decide: build, adjust or choose a different idea.

Week three: build and test

  • Day 15: Build the core of your product.
  • Day 16: Add the instructions page and examples.
  • Day 17: Check licences for every image, font and icon.
  • Day 18: Share with three testers.
  • Day 19: Collect feedback.
  • Day 20: Fix the biggest problems.
  • Day 21: Run through the quality checklist.

Week four: prepare to launch

  • Day 22: Calculate your fees and set your price.
  • Day 23: Draft your sales page and mockups.
  • Day 24: Write your refund policy and delivery email.
  • Day 25: Buy your own product to test delivery.
  • Day 26: List fifty people in your warm network and write your launch messages.
  • Day 27: Set up your tracking sheet.
  • Day 28: Begin your fourteen-day launch plan by sharing helpful content.
  • Day 29: Announce the launch date.
  • Day 30: Review the month and plan your launch week.

28Your Ninety-Day Plan

Days 1 to 30: validate, build and prepare

Complete the thirty-day plan. By day thirty you should have a validated idea, a tested first version, a sales page and a launch plan.

Days 31 to 60: launch and learn

Run your fourteen-day launch. Collect feedback and reviews. Fix problems. Start an email list with a free gift. Review your numbers and write down what you learned.

Days 61 to 90: grow and improve

Promote consistently on one or two platforms. Improve the product using feedback. Create a second product or a bundle based on real requests. Review your income, expenses, time and energy, and decide what to do more of next.

Monthly check-in questions

  • How many people visited my page and how many bought?
  • Where did buyers come from?
  • What questions and feedback did I get?
  • What is my revenue, my expenses and my profit?
  • What did I enjoy, and what drained me?
  • What will I improve or create next?
  • Do I want to continue, adjust or switch direction?

29Questions Girls Ask Me

Can I really make money from digital products as a beginner?

Many people earn something, but I cannot promise results, and many products sell slowly or not at all. Your income depends on your idea, audience, effort, market and timing. Validating before you build and promoting consistently improve your chances.

How long does it take to make my first sale?

Often one to three months from starting, because you need to validate, build and launch. Your first sales usually come from your warm network. Some people are faster, and many are slower.

Do I need to be a designer?

No. Clear, simple and useful beats fancy. Free design tools with templates are enough to begin, and you can learn the basics or hire help later.

What is the best type of digital product to start with?

Templates, printables and short guides are usually the easiest, because they are small, clear and quick to test. Courses and memberships need more effort and are better after you have validated and sold something smaller.

How much should I charge?

Research similar products, count your fees and choose a fair starting price. Many beginners start modest and raise their price as they collect reviews and improve. Never price below your costs.

Should I use a marketplace or my own store?

Many beginners start on a marketplace to learn quickly, then add their own page and email list. Marketplaces bring built-in traffic but charge fees and are crowded. Your own store gives more control but you must bring buyers.

Can I use AI tools to make my product?

You can use them as helpers for brainstorming and drafting, but you must check facts, edit in your own voice and make sure the final product is genuinely useful and original. Read the rules of your marketplace about AI-assisted content.

Can I use free images, fonts and icons?

Only if the licence allows commercial use and the way you plan to use them. Read the terms carefully, keep a record of where each element came from and when in doubt, create your own.

Do I have to pay tax on my sales?

Many countries expect you to report online income and may require registration or tax payments above certain thresholds. Rules differ widely and change. I am not a tax adviser, so check official guidance and consider speaking to a qualified person.

What if someone copies my product?

Keep evidence of your original work, use the platform's reporting tools and check your local rules. Prevention helps: include a clear licence, watermark preview images and keep your source files.

What if I do not have an audience?

You can still sell, through your warm network, marketplaces, helpful content on one or two platforms and building an email list. Start small and grow as people discover you.

What should I do after my first sales?

Ask buyers for feedback, improve the product, ask for reviews, start an email list and plan your second product from what people ask for. Then keep going.

31What To Do Next

You have reached the end of a very long guide, and that tells me something lovely about you: you are willing to build something properly, not just hope.

Here is what I want you to keep. A digital product business is not a trick or a lottery ticket. It is a small shop made of useful things. The women who succeed with it are rarely the most skilled designers or the loudest marketers. They are the ones who found a real problem, tested their idea with real people, built something simple and clear, told the right people honestly and kept improving.

So here is your next step, and it is small. Tonight, list ten things people ask you for help with. Tomorrow, choose one idea and write its promise. This week, speak to three people who might need it. In a month, you could have a tested first version in your hands. In three months, you could have your first buyers, and a clearer picture of what to build next.

When it is slow, remember that slow is still moving. When someone gives you feedback, thank them. When someone buys, deliver beautifully.

When you are ready for more, here are good next steps. How To Create And Sell A Digital Product is a step-by-step companion for your first product. Instagram Pays Too, Sis shows you how to find buyers on Instagram. 30 Passive Income Ideas For Beginners gives a calm look at what is real. Budget Like A Queen helps you manage your money. And our free Academy courses are a gentle place to practise.

I am rooting for you, babe. Begin tonight, go gently and keep going.
